analysis.one_liner: Bars most employers from using job applicants' credit reports in hiring and employment decisions.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the bill on a 32–26 vote in 2019, but the full House never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act to stop consumer reporting agencies from selling an applicant's credit report to employers for hiring, firing, or promotion decisions. Checks would still be allowed when a federal, state, or local law requires them, or for national security investigations, and non-credit background information would be untouched. The aim is to break what the bill calls a catch-22: losing a job or facing a medical bill can wreck someone's credit, and that damaged credit can then keep them from getting hired.
analysis.who_benefits: Job applicants, especially people with damaged credit caused by unemployment, medical debt, or the 2008 financial crisis. The bill's findings cite evidence that credit checks are widespread in ordinary jobs, do not predict job performance, and disproportionately screen out Black and Latino applicants, who on average have lower credit scores.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would generally prohibit consumer reporting agencies from furnishing a consumer report bearing on creditworthiness, standing, or capacity for employment purposes, except when required by law or for a national security investigation.

The bill's findings cite a 2012 study finding that credit history does not actually predict job performance or turnover, while credit reports contain inaccuracies and can be damaged by events outside a person's control, such as a sudden medical expense or job loss.

The findings state that credit checks create a catch-22 for unemployed workers with impaired credit, and that poor credit is associated with unemployment, lack of health coverage, and medical debt, so checks can perpetuate an already precarious situation.

The findings cite research that Black and Latino households on average have lower credit scores, partly because predatory lenders targeted those communities before the 2008 crisis, so credit checks can screen otherwise qualified minority applicants out of jobs.

The bill also bars employers from getting the same information indirectly, forbids passing the cost of any permitted check to the applicant, and does not allow an applicant to waive these protections.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer reporting agencies and background-screening companies that sell employment credit checks would lose that line of business. Some employers would lose a screening tool they use, according to the bill's findings, mainly to reduce theft and embezzlement and to limit liability for negligent hiring.

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings note that organizations said they used credit checks primarily to reduce or prevent theft and embezzlement and to minimize legal liability for negligent hiring; a blanket ban would remove that tool from all employers, including those handling money, though the bill still permits checks when a law requires them.

Credit reports contain other information besides credit history; the bill preserves the ability to use non-credit-related report information, but employers that relied on a single bundled report would need to adjust their screening practices.

The ban takes effect two years after enactment and requires the consumer bureau to write implementing rules within that period, so relief for affected applicants would not be immediate even if it became law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For job seekers, the benefits are substantial: the evidence cited in the bill indicates credit checks do not predict job performance and act as a barrier that hits people already hurt by unemployment, medical bills, or discriminatory lending. The costs fall on credit bureaus and on employers' convenience in screening, which the record suggests is aimed at theft prevention but not supported as a predictor of performance. The exceptions for legally required checks and national security work narrow the ban sensibly.

outcome.mechanism: The Financial Services Committee approved the bill on a 32–26 vote and put it on the House's calendar in November 2019, but the full House never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Al Lawson introduced the bill on July 2, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The committee held a markup on July 11, 2019, and ordered the bill reported as amended by a 32–26 vote.

The committee reported the bill on November 21, 2019, with five additional Democratic cosponsors added, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills awaiting possible House floor action.
No further action was taken; the House never voted on the bill and it expired at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer reporting agencies and background-screening firms keep the employment credit check business, and employers keep the screening tool; job applicants with poor credit remain subject to credit checks when they apply for work.

sides.party_line_note: The committee's 32–26 vote to advance the bill was close and ran largely along party lines in a Democratic-led committee; the published action record does not break down the vote by party.

industries.industry: Consumer reporting agencies and background-screening firms
industries.note: These firms sell employment credit checks to employers, and the bill would cut off that market except for legally required and national security checks. Their revenue from this product comes from access to applicants' credit files, which is exactly what the bill restricts.

industries.industry: Employers using credit checks in hiring
industries.note: Employers would lose a screening tool the bill's findings say is used mainly to reduce theft and limit negligent-hiring liability, though the cited evidence finds credit history does not predict job performance. Some would save screening costs; some would lose a tool they value.
